title: In vivo whole-cell recording from morphologically identified mouse superior colliculus neurons
protocol: Anesthetize the animal with isoflurane.
Weigh the animal to determine the urethane-CPX mixture injection volume.
Calculate the urethane-CPX mixture injection volume as weight of mouse in grams × 0.01 mL.
Inject the calculated volume of urethane-CPX mixture intraperitoneally.
Determine the bupivacaine injection volume based on mouse weight.
Calculate the bupivacaine hydrochloride injection volume as weight of mouse in grams × 1.4 μL.
Inject the calculated volume of bupivacaine subcutaneously.
Place the mouse cage on a constant voltage heating platform.
Prefill a gas anesthesia induction chamber with isoflurane at 4%–5% concentration and flow rate of 0.3 L/min O2.
Place the mouse in the induction chamber and monitor its breathing.
Remove the mouse from the induction chamber once breathing has slowed down.
Assess the depth of anesthesia using the paw withdrawal reflex.
Place the anesthetized mouse on a tissue on the surgery table.
Carefully pinch one of the back paws with a forceps to assess anesthesia depth.
If the mouse shows a withdrawal reflex, place it back in the induction box.
Administer urethane-CPX mixture for long-term anesthesia.
Assess the depth of anesthesia using the paw withdrawal reflex.
Inject the mouse IP with the predetermined volume of urethane-CPX mixture if no withdrawal reflex is detected.
Place the mouse back in its pre-heated cage and wait for the anesthesia to take effect.
After 15 minutes, reassess the animal’s depth of anesthesia using the paw withdrawal reflex.
Administer one dose of additional urethane-CPX mixture if necessary (max 10% of initial dose).
Reassess the paw withdrawal reflex every 15 minutes during preparation to ensure sufficient anesthesia.
Prepare the mouse for head bar placement.
Apply two layers of primer on the dry skull and harden with UV light.
Attach the head bar to the skull using a layer of UV-curing composite.
Secure the head bar with a second layer of composite.
Determine the position of the craniotomy based on coordinates relative to Lambda ('L').
Level the head by placing an object under the snout so that Bregma and Lambda are approximately at equal height.
Cover the temperature sensor with Vaseline and place the probe in the rectum.
Secure the temperature sensor to the table using tape.
Maintain the mouse's body temperature at 37°C.
Apply a drop of silicon oil on both eyes to prevent them from drying out.
Trim the whiskers on both sides.
Trim the whiskers to ensure proper placement of LED goggles or to prevent interference with visual stimulation from haploscope and monitors.
Remove the hair on top of the head using a scalpel dipped in soapy water.
Remove loose hairs with a tissue.
Softly press on the skin to aid shaving.
Shave from the neck forward to the snout, holding the scalpel at a 30° angle to the head surface.
Use small shaving movements for easier removal.
Consider alternatives like an electric hair trimmer or hair removal cream.
Dry the shaved area with an absorbent triangle.
Inject bupivacaine subcutaneously on top of the head for local anesthesia.
Wait more than 5 minutes for the anesthesia to take effect.
Open the head skin and clean the skull.
Remove the skin covering the top of the skull from front to back, starting between the eyes to the back of the skull at the ears.
Remove the remaining tissue from the skull bone using a surgical curette.
Clean the bone with absorbent triangles and a drop of aCSF if necessary.
Wait until bleeding has stopped and the bone is fully dry before proceeding.
Attach the head bar to the skull once the bone is prepared.
Apply a layer of Optibond primer on the skull bone, covering from between the eyes up to the Bregma landmark.
Let the primer etch the bone for 10 seconds.
Harden using UV light for 20 seconds.
Repeat the primer application process one more time.
Secure the head bar to the skull after hardening the second layer of primer.
Apply a layer of UV-curing Kulzer Venus Flow composite on top of the final layer of primer.
Place the head bar on top of the dental composite and harden using UV light for 20 seconds.
Apply dental composite around and on top of the head bar to increase contact with the skull.
Harden using UV light for 20 seconds.
Place the mouse in the electrophysiology rig.
Remove the rectal probe.
Position the mouse on a heating pad in the recording rig.
Secure the head bar to the vertical posts using plastic screws.
Insert the new rectal probe.
Turn on the heating pad control unit.
Maintain the animal temperature at 37°C.
Determine the coordinates of the center of the craniotomy and indicate the location on the skull.
Attach a glass electrode to the pipette holder, positioned perpendicular to the horizontal plane.
Set the micromanipulator coordinates to ‘0’ above the Lambda landmark.
Scratch the skull at the position of the electrode tip to mark the craniotomy site.
Target the SC between -1.1 mm and +0.5 mm in the anteroposterior axis relative to Lambda for adult mice.
For Bregma as a reference, target the SC between -3.1 mm and -4.7 mm in the anteroposterior axis.
In the mediolateral axis, target the SC between 0 and 1.75 mm relative to the midline depending on the anterior-posterior position.
For binocular visual neuron recordings, target the anteromedial part of the SC (0.8 mm–1.0 mm anterior to Lambda, 0.1 mm–0.8 mm lateral to midline).
Perform the craniotomy by making four superficial drill tracks around the determined coordinates.
Frequently apply aCSF kept at room temperature (20°C–22°C) during drilling.
Dry the area using absorbent triangles before continuing to drill.
Stop the drilling process once the skull under the four drill tracks is equally thin.
Carefully grab one corner of the piece of skull to be removed with Dumont type #5/45 bended tip forceps.
Slowly pull off the piece of skull.
Keep the brain tissue moist with aCSF at all times after removing the skull bone.
Remove the dura.
Remove any remaining pieces of skull from the craniotomy with forceps, avoiding touching the brain surface.
Ensure that the edges of the craniotomy are smooth without sharp skull pieces.
Use aCSF to keep the dura mater moist and use absorbent triangles to clean the skull around the craniotomy.
Make a shallow cut in the dura using a 30G needle mounted on a cotton swab, approaching from a near-horizontal angle.
Cut the dura on the far-right (or far-left) side of the craniotomy.
Stop bleedings and keep the brain/dura clean by repeatedly applying aCSF and removing fluid with absorbent triangles.
Position one tip of a fine curved forceps under the dura, avoiding nearby blood vessels.
Carefully remove the dura in one fluent motion.
Keep the dura well hydrated with aCSF and advance removal in small steps if attached to underlying brain tissue.
Optional: Create a well using UV-curing Optibond primer and dental composite around the craniotomy and fill with aCSF to prevent dehydration of the brain tissue.
Prepare the recording and visual stimulation equipment.
Position a chloride-coated reference electrode with thick Ag/AgCl pellet under the neck skin at the back of the incision.
Prepare visual stimuli by applying continuous voltages to the LEDs so that they emit dim light.
Place the LEDs on top of the eyes, ensuring the light illumination is restricted to the eyes only.
Remove continuous voltage from the LEDs after correct positioning.
Place haploscope mirrors in front of the mouse with the snout lightly touching the edge.
Back-fill an electrode with ICS and attach it to the pipette holder.
Establish high positive pressure (>200 mbar) by depressing the plunger of a 10 mL syringe connected to the tubing system.
Position the recording electrode above the SC.
With the patch-clamp amplifier in ‘Voltage Clamp’, run a continuous ‘test-pulse’ protocol (e.g., 50 ms ON/OFF, 10 mV step).
Remove the aCSF from the brain tissue using absorbent triangles.
Position the electrode to approximately 300 μm above the brain surface with the micromanipulator set to coarse speed.
Adjust the micromanipulator to fine speed and advance the electrode vertically downward until the tip reaches the surface.
Monitor the computer screen for a sudden increase in resistance indicating contact between the electrode and the brain surface.
Set the micromanipulator coordinates to ‘0’ when contact is made.
Advance the electrode vertically at approximately 25 μm/s through the tissue until a depth of 200 μm.
Rehydrate the brain tissue by placing a drop of aCSF on the brain surface.
Evaluate the quality of the electrode and replace it if the resistance is lower than 4 MΩ or higher than 7 MΩ.
Advance the electrode to a depth of ∼1,000 μm (∼25 μm/s speed).
Adjust the pressure to ∼20 mbar using the mouth.
Search for neurons in voltage-clamp mode, monitoring the current during a test pulse.
Determine compensation for the voltage drop due to series resistance using negative current pulses in current-clamp mode.
Use bridge balance (BB) control to adjust for series resistance compensation.
Inject active current to compensate for input circuit and electrode capacitance using capacitance compensation (Cap. comp.).
Advance the electrode in steps of 2 μm (at a speed of 2–4 μm/s) while monitoring changes in current.
Frequently adjust the pipette offset to zero and maintain pressure at ∼20 mbar.
Observe sharp (>50%) drops in test pulse current amplitude for indications of neuron proximity.
Monitor 'vertical wobble' in test pulse current amplitude as an additional indication of neuron proximity.
Establish a gigaseal connection by advancing another 2–4 μm upon observing indications of proximity.
Quickly release positive pressure and apply mild negative pressure (less than -15 mbar) after establishing proximity.
Set the command voltage to -70 mV early in the process to aid in establishing the gigaseal.
Gradually reduce negative pressure as resistance approaches 1 GΩ.
Form an ideal gigaseal within a few seconds after releasing pressure and starting suction.
Discard neurons that do not reach a gigaseal or if the formation takes longer than 30 seconds.
Replace the patch electrode and repeat steps for forming a gigaseal if no seal is formed.
Compensate for fast and slow capacitance transients in the cell-attached configuration after forming a gigaseal.
Apply short pulses of negative suction to rupture the cell membrane and transition into whole-cell configuration.
Start with gentle suction pulses and increase as required for membrane rupture.
Record a voltage step protocol to determine the access resistance, input resistance, and cell membrane capacitance values.
Optimize amplifier settings and characterize the neuron in current clamp mode.
Set the patch-clamp amplifier to ‘Current Clamp’.
Run a negative current step protocol (e.g., 10 ms ON/OFF, -100 pA).
Use the ‘Tuning’ controls for adjustment.
Compensate for the voltage drop due to series resistance by adjusting the ‘Bridge Balance’ controls.
Apply ‘Capacitance Neutralisation/Compensation’ to compensate for the capacitance of the amplifier and electrode.
Increase compensation until an overshoot at the onset of the voltage change to a current pulse becomes visible.
Avoid overcompensating which will lead to oscillations and potentially the loss of the recording.
Characterize the voltage response of the cell using a current step protocol comprising of both negative and positive current injections (e.g., 500 ms ON/OFF, -200 pA to +600 pA with 50 pA steps).
Prepare responses to visual stimulation.
Record neuronal responses during alternating visual stimulation of the left eye.
Record neuronal responses during alternating visual stimulation of the right eye.
Record neuronal responses during bilateral visual stimulation of both eyes simultaneously.
Use 20 ms LED flashes for visual stimulation.
Maintain an inter-trial interval (ITI) of 2,980 ms between each stimulus condition.
Repeat the stimulation process with 50 repetitions per stimulus condition.

For visual stimulation using the haploscope and monitors, present stimuli for 1.5 seconds followed by an inter-stimulus interval (ITI) of 2.5 seconds, repeating this process for 50 repetitions per stimulus condition.
Allow sufficient time between each stimulus to prevent influence from preceding stimuli.
Retract the electrode carefully.
Switch the system to voltage clamp mode at -70 mV and release any air pressure applied.
Run a continuous 'test-pulse' protocol (e.g., 50 ms ON/OFF, 10 mV step) to ensure access to the neuron.
Initially retract the pipette by 4-6 μm and wait for 5 seconds to allow the neuron to recover.
Slowly retract the pipette at a rate of 2 μm per 3 seconds while monitoring the current trace closely.
Continue retraction slowly until the tip of the pipette is more than 200 μm away from the neuron, then proceed with normal speed.
Prepare the perfusion setup.
Fill one 50 mL syringe with 30 mL of 1× PBS.
Fill one 50 mL syringe with 30 mL of 4% PFA solution.

Place surgical scissors, iris scissors, spatula, forceps (Dumont type #3), Graefe forceps, hemostat, Castroviejo scissors, drip tray with dissecting board, four 25G needles, tissues, and a butterfly needle by the perfusion area.
Fill a 15 mL Falcon tube with 4% PFA solution for post-fixation of the brain.
Connect the butterfly needle to the syringe containing PBS.
Rinse the tubing with PBS to ensure no air bubbles are present.
Anesthetize the mouse with an overdose of pentobarbitone solution.
Inject pentobarbitone solution (150 mg/kg) IP.
Calculate the volume to inject using the formula: weight of mouse in grams × 0.0025 mL.
Inject 0.05 mL of pentobarbitone solution in a 20 g mouse.
Assess the depth of anesthesia using the paw withdrawal reflex after 3 min.
Inject additional pentobarbitone solution if the withdrawal reflex persists.
Perform transcardial perfusion.
Place the mouse on its back and secure the limbs in an extended position by pinning to a dissecting board with 25-gauge needle tips.
Open the abdominal wall below the rib cage using forceps and iris scissors.
Carefully cut open the diaphragm in a lateral direction and cut upward through the ribs on both sides.
Attach the hemostat to the skin flap and place above the mouse to keep the rib cage open.
Expose the heart and insert the butterfly needle into the left ventricle.
Make a cut in the right atrium with the Castroviejo scissors.
Exert moderate pressure on the plunger to rinse the heart and blood vessels with PBS.
Assess the liver color for successful perfusion after PBS injection.
Connect syringe with 4% PFA if initial perfusion is completed and continue perfusion.
Assess muscle contractions in limbs post-perfusion as an indication of effective perfusion.
Work in a laboratory safety cabinet and wear appropriate PPE when handling PFA.
Use a peristaltic perfusion pump for consistent and controlled flow during perfusion.
Remove needles holding the mouse to the dissecting board.
Separate head from body using surgical scissors.
Cut through skin from neck to snout and pull skin aside.
Position iris scissors tips in eye sockets and cut between eyes.
Hold head so that eyes face the researcher.
Insert one tip of the scissors in the cut between the eye sockets.
Cut through the skull via the left lateral side of the head from anterior to posterior, maintaining a dorsal position.
Use Graefe forceps to remove the skull by inserting under the left side and pulling over to the right side.
Remove remaining pieces of skull and loose pieces of dura mater.
Position spatula under the brain and lift out while inverting the skull.
Cut through the optic nerves using iris scissors.
Place the brain in a 15 mL Falcon tube containing 4% PFA.
Post-fix the brain between 2 and 24 hours at 4°C if perfusion was not optimal, or store long-term at -20°C after fully sinking in 30% sucrose solution for 24 hours.
Prepare the cryostat with a chamber temperature of −20°C.
Secure a cutting blade in the cryostat blade holder.
Fill a 12-well plate with 1× PBS using a Pasteur pipette.
Fill a petri dish with a layer of 1× PBS.
Take the brain out of the 30% sucrose solution and place it on a filter paper in a petri dish.
Make a cut perpendicular to the horizontal plane to remove the anterior part of the brain.
Cut off the cerebellum and brainstem at -5 to -6 mm from Bregma.
Place the brain in a cryomold and immerse in Tissue-Tek Optimal Cutting Temperature (OCT) compound.
Remove the frozen brain from the cryomold.
Apply a layer of OCT on the cryostat chuck and place the frozen brain on the chuck.
Apply a layer of OCT around the edges of the brain.
Place the chuck in the cryostat chamber and wait until frozen.
Position the chuck firmly onto the moving platform in the cryostat chamber.
Position the cutting blade close to the brain and start slicing from the posterior end of the brain forward, until the posterior end of SC is reached around -4.8 mm from Bregma.
Cut 100 μm coronal brain sections and transport the slices from the cryostat chamber to a 12-well plate using a fine brush.
Slice until the anterior end of SC is reached -3 mm to Bregma.
Place the slices in order of sectioning.
Wash sections 5 × 5 min in 1 mL 1× PBS per well in a 12-well plate placed on an orbital shaker.
Place sections in 1% H2O2 in 1× PBS for 15 minutes to block endogenous peroxidase activity.
Wash sections 3 times for 10 minutes each in 1× PBS.
Place sections in 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA) and 0.3% Triton X-100 in 1× PBS for 1 hour at room temperature.
Incubate sections overnight (16–24 hours) in ABC solution on an orbital shaker at room temperature (20°C–22°C).
Wash sections 3 times for 5 minutes each in 1× PBS.
Prepare the 3,3′-Diaminobenzidine (DAB) solution as per kit instructions.
Incubate the sections in the DAB solution for 5–10 minutes on an orbital shaker at room temperature (20°C–22°C).
Wash the slices 3 times for 5 minutes each in 1× PBS.
Mount the slices on microscope slides and cover using curing mounting medium (VectaMount) and a coverslip.
Work with DAB in a laboratory safety cabinet.
Wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) when handling DAB.
Discard used DAB solution in a bottle containing 5% sodium hypochlorite (bleach).
Follow laboratory procedures for the disposal of hazardous chemicals.
